Senses.Explanation: In Caodong technical discourse, lord and minister name a relational configuration used to explain upright and inclined positions and their interaction. Caoshan Benji maps lord to the upright position and minister to the inclined, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister accord. A later Caoshan quotation repeats that mapping. Juelang Daosheng equates arriving within both with lord and minister according. Yinqian identifies the Caodong house through their accord. Langting Ting disputes the later classification of Caoshan's answers as five lord-and-minister positions. Shixi Xinyue sets the five positions beside Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Shaoyuan says the five positions are all penetrated when host and guest accord. These uses establish a technical relational family while preserving disagreement about its historical systematization.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去，空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Wuyi Yuanlai later quotes the inherited answer among cases he explicitly calls “without semantic flavor.” Yongjue Yuanxian raises the same old answer, appraises the inherited cluster, and contrasts it with answers of his own. Senses.Explanation: A fierce tiger does not eat meat that submits before it pictures the tiger declining prey already lying prostrate. Gulin Qingmao pairs the line with a fine hawk that does not strike a dead rabbit. Tian'an Sheng repeats the pair, then says that if the listener brings a Linji shout he will block the listener's throat, and if the listener brings a Deshan staff he will break it in two. When a monk tells Liangting Jingting, 'I knew it,' Liangting gives the tiger line; the monk then shouts, and Liangting calls the shout excessive. Zuliang Chaoqi calls for anyone willing to risk his life before Xuansha's released tiger; when nobody comes forward, he gives the line and leaves. Xiaoyan Debao raises Yunmen Wenyan's encounter with an approaching monk, criticizes Yunmen's handling, and places the phrase in his own counterfactual response. The retained lamp witness preserves Jingqing Daofu giving the saying after the monk says that he has failed or disappointed Jingqing. These passages repeatedly place prostrate or already-yielding prey beside a response, challenge, or exchange that has stopped short.
